Important limit first: I could not verify a release-by-release diff here. File reading and network access were unavailable, so the specific SCOPe release in which any 1acc boundary edit appeared is stated below as a candidate, not as fact. The parts I am confident about are the SCOP 1.75 architecture and what it implies.

What SCOP 1.75 had. PDB 1acc is the Petosa (1997) structure of the anthrax protective antigen monomer, a single long chain A that SCOP 1.75 cut into four domains, d1acca1 through d1acca4, matching the four-domain description in the original paper. The four pieces do not sit together in the hierarchy. Domain 4 is an immunoglobulin-like beta-sandwich and lands in the large all-beta Ig-like fold region (SCOP b.1). Domain 2 is the beta-barrel-forming core, widely noted as structurally similar to the aerolysin and Clostridium perfringens epsilon-toxin group of beta-barrel pore formers; whether SCOPe places it in a shared superfamily with them or in a protective-antigen-specific superfamily under a shared fold is exactly the assignment to check in the release files. Domain 1 is a calcium-binding alpha-plus-beta domain, and domain 3 is a small alpha-plus-beta oligomerization domain. One chain therefore contributes to four separate lineages.

Approximate boundaries in PA83 numbering:

| Domain | Residues |
|---|---|
| 1a | 1-167 |
| 1b | 168-258 |
| 2 | 259-487 |
| 3 | 488-595 |
| 4 | 596-735 |

The change, and how to confirm it. The candidate edit is at domain 1: SCOP 1.75 treated residues 1-258 as one unit, while the biologically meaningful split is 1a and 1b either side of the protease-sensitive loop near residue 167, since 1a is released on activation and 1b stays with the oligomer. A second candidate is a boundary shift at the domain 2 and 3 junction, because domain 2 has a long beta-hairpin that projects away from its own barrel. Verification needs release-specific evidence I did not have: the parseable dir.cla and dir.des files for SCOP 1.75 versus SCOPe 1.75A/B/C and 2.01 through 2.08, plus the per-sunid history page, which records whether a domain was renumbered, resplit, or moved. Note also that SCOPe after 1.75 classifies most new entries automatically by inheritance from manually curated parents, so old manual definitions for an entry like 1acc often persist unchanged while newer homologs inherit boundaries from them. That asymmetry, not a visible edit, is frequently the real source of inconsistent boundaries across a superfamily.

What it reveals about domains as evolutionary modules. Protective antigen is a mosaic, not a single module. Domain 2 shares ancestry with a family of beta-barrel pore formers; domain 4 belongs to a fold so large and so often convergent that membership carries almost no ancestry signal; domains 1 and 3 have their own separate histories. The recombining unit is the one that recurs in other proteins, which is not always the most compact unit a curator would carve out by eye. Domain definitions are therefore hypotheses that get revised as new structures arrive, and a release-pinned identifier is the only stable way to refer to one.

How it should affect homology searches. Search and annotate per domain, never per chain. A full-chain alignment against 1acc produces inflated global similarity and tempts whole-protein function transfer, which is unsafe here: a hit to domain 2 supports shared beta-barrel architecture at superfamily strength and nothing about receptor binding, and a hit to domain 4 is fold-level at best and should not be read as homology at all. Parse the query into domains before profile search, pin the SCOPe release and the ASTRAL subset used, and check whether 1acc domains are even the chosen representatives at 40 percent or 95 percent identity, since a different family member may be the representative and a better template. For structure work, remember 1acc is the soluble monomer; prepore and pore conformations differ enough that template choice changes the model. Confirm any transfer with independent evidence: hidden Markov model profile hits with per-domain coverage, conservation of the specific binding or oligomerization residues, and genomic context.
